# Public API

<!-- Generated by `npm run train` from the sources each rule cites. To change a rule for good, change its source or say so in training/feedback.md; the next training run regenerates this file. -->

- **When a public, replaceable service must enforce a policy (especially a security policy), put that policy behind its own public interface that replacements resolve. Register its internal default with `TryAdd`, and don't put the policy inside the internal default implementation or inside a data-supplying resolver.** If the policy is internal, every replacement has to reimplement it or silently skips it, and the copies drift. If only a concrete class is exposed, the policy's dependencies become part of the public API. *Check:* Look for policy logic (combining bounds, enforcing requirements, choosing credentials) that lives only in the internal default of a public replacement point, in internal helpers, or in a replaceable resolver. Also look for public concrete classes used as the seam and for defaults registered unconditionally. <sub>Identity ADR-1155; Identity ADR-1158; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **An extension seam that takes part in a security decision (a login gate, session validator, claims or response contributor) may only reject, end or add. It must never skip or weaken a built-in check, and a contributor must be refused changes to reserved anchoring entries (such as `iss`, `sub`, `sid`, `auth_time`, `acr`, `amr`) and refused names that were already added.** Built-in invariants such as callback binding, cookie attributes, CSRF checks, allow-lists and the claims that tie a session to authentication must hold whatever a plugin does. *Check:* Look at gate, validator and contributor contracts and their call sites. Flag a result that can bypass or override built-in validation, and add/remove APIs that don't check a reserved list or duplicate names. <sub>Identity docs/backend-for-frontend.md; Identity ADR-1290</sub>
- **Make a security-relevant flag or decision on an extensible type that replaceable handlers or registered descriptors construct either a required member (positional or `required`) or a member whose default is the safe value. Set it explicitly on every built-in descriptor.** An optional `init` property that defaults to the permissive value lets a custom handler or contributed descriptor fail open with no warning at compile time or start-up, for example private key material treated as public, or logout without a prompt. *Check:* Look for new bool or enum members on public results, DTOs or descriptors returned or registered by extensibility points that control a security or storage behaviour and default to the unsafe value through an optional `init` property. *Note:* This doesn't cover ordinary optional inputs. Don't ask for `required` on an optional `init` property whose default the library supplies on purpose: the convention is that optional inputs are `init` properties with library defaults. <sub>Identity ADR-1380; Identity outcomes of #504; Identity outcomes of #531; Identity outcomes of #554; Identity outcomes of #724</sub>
- **Model a one-time secret reveal as its own response type (the material-free resource plus the material). Keep secret read and list resources metadata-only, and expose a public key through a separate read-only sub-resource.** An optional, usually-null material field on the type every read returns turns leakage prevention into a review discipline. A separate type makes every place a secret can appear structurally visible. *Check:* Look for nullable secret, plaintext, key-material, JWK or PEM properties added to a shared resource, read DTO or list item, and for one response type reused by revealing and non-revealing endpoints. <sub>Identity ADR-1050; Identity ADR-1268</sub>
- **In production code, start every type and member at the narrowest visibility that works, and widen to `public` only for a consumer contract, an entry point or data that consumers construct. Keep the concrete `Default*` implementation behind a public interface `internal`, keep job types internal to the package that produces them, and never make a member public (or unsealed, or `virtual`) only so a test can reach or mock it.** An accidental `public` is a contract that must be supported until the next major version. Only the interface or dispatch port is the contract. *Check:* Look for new public types or members with no consumer reason, public `Default*` classes registered in DI, public job types, and types widened to public or left unsealed next to new tests that use them. *Note:* Tests reach internals through `InternalsVisibleTo` (see the InternalsVisibleTo rule). <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity csharp-tests.instructions.md; Identity docs/backend-for-frontend.md; Identity ADR-1242</sub>
- **Grant `InternalsVisibleTo` only to test (`*Tests`) and benchmark (`*.Benchmarks`) assemblies and to `DynamicProxyGenAssembly2`, never to another production assembly. Production assemblies collaborate through public contracts.** Coupling production assemblies through internals bypasses the contract. `DynamicProxyGenAssembly2` lets Moq proxy internal types. *Check:* Look for `InternalsVisibleTo` attributes or csproj items that name a production assembly, or that name a test assembly that doesn't exist. <sub>Identity convention-audit.instructions.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity csharp-tests.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, treat a vocabulary (kinds, types, modes, scopes, formats, methods, reasons, statuses, stages, audit outcomes, categories and similar) as open by default. Model it as `public const string` names in a static class, documented as the known values and compared ordinally, or as registered descriptors or strategies resolved by name through a catalog (`TryGet`-style lookup).** An enum, a switch over members or a closed hierarchy fixes the members at compile time, so a consumer or sibling package can't add one without editing the library. *Check:* Look for a new `enum`, closed list or switch over a vocabulary another package could plausibly extend, for string-name comparisons that don't use `StringComparison.Ordinal`/`StringComparer.Ordinal`, and for docs that claim the names are exhaustive. Failure-code and audit vocabularies use lower-case (snake_case for failure codes) string values. <sub>Identity ADR-1150; Identity ADR-1119; Identity ADR-1246; Identity ADR-1278; Identity docs/audit-records.md; Identity docs/backend-for-frontend.md; Identity convention-audit.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity repository.instructions.md</sub>
- **Declare an `enum` only when all three conditions hold: its members are fixed by something that can't grow without this library changing (a finite enumeration of an external specification the library implements in full, the outcome set of one library-owned operation, or a mirror of a framework type); no other package could ever need another member; and a new member would need a library change anyway. Never use `[Flags]` or bitmasks for a vocabulary that may grow.** Closing a vocabulary is the exception and must be justifiable. Asking only whether the package owns today's members led to enums that shut out extensions. A `[Flags]` enum closes both the bit space and the meaning of every combination. *Check:* For each new or changed enum, try to state the three-part justification, and ask whether a package other than this one could ever need to add a member. Grep for `[Flags]` and for switches or masks that encode relationships among a vocabulary's members. <sub>Identity ADR-1150; Identity convention-audit.instructions.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't ask to replace an enum with string names when it passes the three-part closed test, for example when it mirrors a finite RFC registry or parameter set, mirrors a framework type, lists the forms a library-owned converter can handle, or is the outcome set of one library-owned operation, or when a decision record explains why it is closed.** A set that really is closed gains exhaustiveness checking and type safety from an enum. Modeling it as strings adds validation and gives no extensibility in return. *Check:* Before reporting an enum as a closed vocabulary, check where its members come from and look for a decision record that justifies keeping it closed. <sub>Identity ADR-1150; Identity outcomes of #554</sub>
- **Consumers of an open code vocabulary (such as policy error codes or failure codes) must handle unknown values instead of assuming that only the built-in values exist.** A replacement implementation or extension may report codes of its own. *Check:* Flag exhaustive switches or mappings over open code vocabularies that have no fallback for unknown values. <sub>Identity ADR-1236; Identity ADR-1278</sub>
- **Don't model an open set of event, record or request types as a closed polymorphic hierarchy, such as `[JsonDerivedType]` attributes listed on the base type or a single type with a kind enum. Use an abstract base that carries the shared members, with sealed subclasses that packages can add.** A package that adds an event or a grant would otherwise have to edit the library. *Check:* Look for `[JsonDerivedType]` lists on event or audit base types, single request types that branch on a kind enum, and subclasses that should be sealed but aren't. <sub>Identity ADR-1283; Identity ADR-1285</sub>
- **Don't add a capability-specific method to a shared base abstraction. Expose one generic entry point that takes a caller-supplied subtype, and let each capability own its type, constants and a convenience extension method.** A per-capability method puts one capability's shape on a general abstraction. One generic entry point serves every capability. *Check:* Look for new methods on a shared interface or base class named after one feature or resource type, and for capability-specific event types or constants declared in the base package. <sub>Identity ADR-1057</sub>
- **To add an operation that only some implementations of a contract support, define a derived interface with real members. Don't add a parameter to the base method that some implementations must throw for, and don't add an empty marker interface, including one that only tags an implementation that configuration selects by name (resolve that implementation by name through a catalog).** A parameter the base contract doesn't need forces implementations that give it no meaning to throw, and a marker interface adds a type without adding a rule. *Check:* Look for new parameters on shared interface methods that some implementations reject with `NotSupportedException`/`ArgumentException`, and for new empty interfaces used for capability checks or role tagging. <sub>Identity ADR-1414; Identity ADR-1260</sub>
- **Take an open-vocabulary strategy (such as an encoding) by name and resolve it through the registered collection, rather than taking a strategy instance. Take a hash algorithm as `System.Security.Cryptography.HashAlgorithmName`, not as a library enum or a custom algorithm type.** Settings and stored records carry names, and one registered collection is the single place that validates the set. The framework already owns the open hash-algorithm vocabulary. *Check:* Look for public methods that take a strategy instance where callers would hold a configured or persisted name, and for hashing APIs whose algorithm parameter is an enum. <sub>Identity ADR-1190</sub>
- **Don't add `bool` or `enum` parameters whose only job is to switch a method between behaviors. Split them into intention-revealing methods, strategies, or separate contracts (for example, one validator per token type rather than a mode flag). A `bool` carried as data is fine.** Flag parameters hide intent at call sites and make the contract's requirements conditional. *Check:* Look for `bool` or `enum` parameters or options that branch a whole method or validator into a different behavior. <sub>Identity convention-audit.instructions.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1274</sub>
- **Make required inputs constructor parameters and optional inputs nullable `init` properties that the library resolves to a default (failing closed) when null. Never add an optional value as a new constructor parameter, a defaulted public-constructor parameter (exception constructors included) or a new positional parameter of a public record.** A new constructor or positional parameter changes the binary signature and breaks every `new T(...)` call site and serializer. It also forces callers to pass explicit nulls. Resolving the default inside the library keeps it out of consumer code. *Check:* Look for public constructors or positional records that gain a parameter (often visible as call sites now passing `null`), `= null` defaults on public constructor parameters, and optional properties that aren't nullable or that leave consumers to supply the default. <sub>Identity docs/api-compatibility.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1025; Identity outcomes of #572; Identity outcomes of #584</sub>
- **Pass an optional, growing set of selection criteria as a `readonly record struct` with non-required `init` properties, and model request, command and validator inputs as init-only records (with `required` for required fields) rather than positional constructors or loose parameters. Keep a required identity key that is the operation's subject as a positional parameter, and take pagination as one page-request object (cursor plus limit).** Store and service interfaces are implemented by consumers, so a new positional parameter breaks every implementer and caller. A required key isn't a growing filter, and a positional (cursor, limit) pair can't gain a sort direction without a signature change. *Check:* Look for methods gaining another optional filter parameter, criteria or request types with positional constructors, required ids moved into optional DTO properties, and paged methods with separate cursor and limit parameters. <sub>Identity ADR-1080; Identity ADR-1274; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Allow optional parameters on at most one overload of a method name, and express an optional tail as explicit overloads with and without the argument.** Several overloads with optional parameters cause ambiguous and fragile binding (RS0026). *Check:* Look for several overloads of one name that each have default parameter values. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't ask for default values on parameters that come before a required trailing `CancellationToken`, and don't report call sites that pass each of those arguments explicitly, `null` included. Don't report a `CancellationToken` that the repository's conventions require as unused or dead.** No optional parameter may come before the token, so every caller passes each input explicitly. A parameter required by convention isn't dead code. *Check:* Before reporting positional `null` arguments, lost defaults or an unused token, confirm whether the token is the convention-required last parameter. <sub>Identity outcomes of #753</sub>
- **Don't put a `CancellationToken` parameter on audit-recorder or post-commit effect methods, and don't add one that the implementation ignores.** A token parameter invites callers to pass the request's token, which can cancel work that must run after the commit. An ignored parameter misleads readers. *Check:* Look for recorder or post-commit effect interfaces and methods that declare a `CancellationToken`. *Note:* This is a deliberate exception to the usual rule that async methods take a token. When reviewing these methods, don't report a missing token parameter. <sub>Identity ADR-1351</sub>
- **In production code, make data, options, context, event and result types `sealed`, with get-only or `init` members. Use interfaces only for replaceable DI seams or read-only slices, not for data or persisted payloads, and keep persisted payloads as concrete data-contract records with pluggability at the store interface. Otherwise seal a type by derivation intent: leave an abstraction meant as an extension point unsealed.** Data should be immutable and not open to extension by accident. Pluggability belongs at the store seam, not on the payload. *Check:* Look for unsealed data, options or event classes, settable members, interfaces declared over data or persisted records, and extension-point bases that have been sealed. *Note:* Before asking for a type to be sealed, or deciding it can't be, grep for `:\s*TypeName\b` to confirm it is really a base class. A property of that type is composition and doesn't block sealing. <sub>Identity convention-audit.instructions.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1051</sub>
- **Keep result and validation-result types as plain data that consumers and test doubles can construct. Put follow-up operations such as commit or record on the service that produced the result.** A follow-up operation on the result makes it hold services and state, and splits the logic across two places. *Check:* Flag result or DTO types that gain methods or fields holding stores, registrations or other services. <sub>Identity ADR-1274</sub>
- **Use read-only collection interfaces (`IReadOnlyList<T>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, `IReadOnlySet<T>`, `params IEnumerable<T>`) for parameters and computed return values. Expose stored collection properties as concrete types, never `IList<T>`, and store a collection that the type validates as `ImmutableArray<T>` or a frozen collection, copying any collection the caller assigns.** Signatures stay flexible while storage stays concrete and owned. A stored caller-owned list can be mutated after it was validated, and returning a `List<T>` exposes mutable storage that no caller needs. *Check:* Look for `List<T>`/`T[]` parameters or returns that callers only read, `IList<T>` properties, `params T[]`, and validated `IReadOnlyList`/`IReadOnlyDictionary` properties assigned without a copy. <sub>Identity convention-audit.instructions.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #548; Identity outcomes of #554</sub>
- **Don't pass or return `null` where an empty form exists. Make a collection parameter non-nullable and have callers pass `[]`, unless null means something different from empty.** Null collections force null checks and null-handling branches, and cause NullReferenceExceptions. *Check:* Look for methods returning null for a collection, and for nullable collection parameters that callers pass `null` to. Confirm that null carries no distinct meaning before reporting. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #741</sub>
- **Don't make a contract field nullable when every caller would then apply the same fallback. Compute the fallback on the server and make the field required. When a public contract property does become nullable, or starts being null on a new path, say when it is null in its XML remarks.** A nullable field makes every caller repeat the fallback, and implementers written against the old non-null contract will dereference null. *Check:* Look for new nullable response properties whose docs or callers all substitute the same default, and for properties changed from `T` to `T?` without remarks. <sub>Identity ADR-1161; Identity outcomes of #600</sub>
- **When a boolean guard (such as `IsConfigured` or `IsValid`) guarantees that a nullable member is non-null, annotate it with `[MemberNotNullWhen]` or `[NotNullWhen]` so callers can read the member without `!` or a second null check.** Nullable analysis then knows the guard's guarantee. *Check:* Look for guard properties or methods next to the nullable members they check that lack the attribute, and for callers that use `!` or re-check after the guard. *Note:* Don't ask for such a flag to be derived from another member (for example `FailureCode is null`) when the getter can't prove the attribute (CS8775). A private constructor and factories keep the flag consistent. <sub>Identity review of #833; Identity outcomes of #554</sub>
- **When a method's behaviour or output form changes, give it a name that states the new form instead of keeping the old name and signature. To make parsing stricter or broader, add a new, separately named accessor instead of changing what an existing shared accessor accepts.** An unchanged name and signature keeps compiling for existing callers, so the break shows up only at run time. *Check:* Look for public methods whose signature is unchanged but whose output or accepted inputs changed meaning. <sub>Identity outcomes of #531; Identity ADR-1123</sub>
- **When a wrapper is documented to behave like an existing parse API, delegate to that API so it honors every option, instead of copying a subset of the options by hand. Let a constructor adopt an already in-memory value (`JsonElement`, `JsonObject`, a collection), and reserve a static `Parse(string)` for reading text.** Copying options by hand silently drops some, such as `AllowDuplicateProperties`. Keeping adoption separate from parsing makes the cost and failure mode of each clear. *Check:* Look for options objects translated field by field into another options type, constructors that parse JSON strings, and `Parse` methods that take an already-parsed value. <sub>Identity review of #420; Identity ADR-1119</sub>
- **Use a writable `Span<T>`/`Memory<T>` parameter only as a destination whose size the caller knows before the call, and return the count written when output can be shorter. When a public method writes into a caller-supplied span, also give it an overload that writes to a generic `ref TWriter destination` with `where TWriter : IBufferWriter<byte>, allows ref struct`, plus a matching `GetByteCount` sizing method. Never take a plain `IBufferWriter<byte>` parameter.** Callers must be able to size destinations and know how much was written. The generic writer form saves callers from renting buffers and supports stack-only writers. *Check:* Check new methods with writable span outputs for a sizing member or fixed size, a returned count and a writer overload. Flag output parameters typed as plain `IBufferWriter<byte>`. <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity review of #375; Identity review of #382</sub>
- **Order write and copy method parameters with the source or input first and the destination (writer, buffer writer, output span) last.** This keeps new APIs consistent with existing ones such as `Decode(source, ref destination)`. *Check:* Look for new methods whose destination parameter comes before the value being written. <sub>Identity review of #382</sub>
- **Expose a key's public half through a SubjectPublicKeyInfo writer that is generic over `IBufferWriter<byte>`, not through `AsymmetricAlgorithm`.** `AsymmetricAlgorithm` ties the contract to the RSA and ECDSA families and can't hold Edwards-curve or post-quantum keys. *Check:* Look for new base-class or interface members that return or accept `AsymmetricAlgorithm` as the generic way to get at a public key. <sub>Identity ADR-1104</sub>
- **When an extension applies to two unrelated receiver interfaces that one concrete type implements (for example `IDictionary<,>` and `IReadOnlyDictionary<,>`), write one extension on their common base and fast-path the specific types inside it.** An overload for each interface is ambiguous (CS0121) on a type that implements both. *Check:* Look for parallel extension overloads on sibling interfaces that share a base. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't add a parameter for a value the method can derive from `HttpContext`, such as the endpoint name. Read it from `HttpContext.GetEndpoint()` metadata (`IEndpointNameMetadata.EndpointName`, else `DisplayName`).** A redundant parameter lets callers drift from the one rule for deriving the value. *Check:* Look for methods that take both an `HttpContext` and a request-derived argument, and for duplicated helpers that read endpoint metadata. <sub>Identity review of #382</sub>
- **Never share one type between two packages that version independently. Keep the type in the package whose capability it is, or duplicate it on purpose.** Shared types couple independent version lines, and a type belongs with its capability so consumers get it from one package. *Check:* Look for linked source files, and for a type defined in one package and consumed as a contract by an independently versioned one. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1500</sub>
- **Give a library's public types a shallow, stable namespace under the root that doesn't change when a file moves. Internal types use a namespace that matches their folder.** Public namespaces are part of the contract. *Check:* Look for public types whose namespace mirrors deep folders, and for namespace changes on moved public types. *Note:* Don't report a public sub-namespace that is a purpose namespace shared across an `.Abstractions`/implementation pair (such as `.Validation`), or one that matches the package's other public types and mirrors a sibling package's equivalent type. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #529; Identity outcomes of #554</sub>
- **Mark a type that is public only so the project's own assemblies can share it with `[EditorBrowsable(EditorBrowsableState.Never)]`, and open its `<summary>` with "This API supports the {product} infrastructure and is not intended to be used directly from your code."** This signals that the type isn't a supported consumer contract. *Check:* Look for infrastructure-only public types that lack the attribute or the summary text. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, annotate a public type that reflection, DI, the options binder or a serializer consumes with JetBrains `[PublicAPI]`, and never apply `[PublicAPI]` to an internal type.** It states intent and silences unused-member noise. On an internal type it wrongly presents the type as public surface. *Check:* Look for serializer- or DI-consumed public types without `[PublicAPI]`, and for `[PublicAPI]` on internal types. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Make service contracts public interfaces with internal `Default*` implementations, and make options classes sealed with an accompanying validator.** These are the conventions for NCodeGroup library packages. *Check:* Look for public implementation classes of service interfaces, implementations not named `Default*`, unsealed options classes, and options without a validator. <sub>Identity docs/backend-for-frontend.md</sub>
- **Don't ask to make internal, or to move into an Abstractions package, a public registration marker type that a library's `AddX()` method returns. Don't claim a public overload serves only tests until a search of production code finds no callers.** The marker is a public return type by convention, and an overload that looks like a thin wrapper may be the shape most production code uses. *Check:* Before reporting, check whether the type is the return type of a public `AddX` method, and search production code for callers of the member. <sub>Identity outcomes of #600; Identity outcomes of #592</sub>
- **A create endpoint's request must not accept an identifier for the resource it creates. The server mints an opaque identifier and returns it in the `201` body and the `Location` header. Never expose internal surrogate keys (database identity or snowflake `Id` columns) in responses, routes or cursors.** Caller-chosen ids get tied to every reference and push format, validation and collision handling onto every caller. Surrogate keys leak internals and aren't public identities. *Check:* Look for create DTOs or handlers that read the new resource's id from the body, create responses missing the id or `Location`, surrogate `Id` properties in response models and numeric key route parameters. *Note:* A name chosen by the creator, where the name is the resource (such as a tenant name), is the exception. <sub>Identity ADR-1014</sub>
- **Take a parent resource reference from the route, never from the request body.** Authorization and tenant confinement apply to the route, and a body value could contradict it. *Check:* Look for nested-endpoint request DTOs that carry a parent id the handler uses in place of the route value. <sub>Identity ADR-1014</sub>
- **A management endpoint that acts on an owner must answer 404 for an unknown owner, and must never lazily create resources (such as keys) for it. Answer 404 and 409 from the rows loaded before the write, let the store's own failures propagate, and return every error as a problem document (never a bare `TypedResults.NotFound()`).** Lazy creation plants state for owners that don't exist, and translating store failures into conflicts misreports them. *Check:* Look for get-or-create calls that run before the owner's existence is checked, catch blocks that turn store exceptions into 404 or 409, and bare status results without a problem body. <sub>Identity ADR-1407; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Answer an API authentication challenge with 401 and a forbid with 403 as `application/problem+json`, never with a 302 redirect to a login page.** fetch/XHR callers can't follow a login redirect, and SPAs rely on 401 to mean there is no session. *Check:* Look for API endpoints or authentication handlers that redirect on challenge or forbid. <sub>Identity docs/backend-for-frontend.md</sub>
- **Declare every status a minimal API route can answer with `.Produces`/`.ProducesProblem`/`ProducesValidationProblem()`, unless a group-level declaration already covers it: 401/403 as applicable, 404/409 the handler returns, 412 when it saves a unit of work it doesn't retry (inserts included) or checks `If-Match`, 415 for a `[FromBody]` parameter, `ProducesValidationProblem()` for a validation 400, and 400 declared once for a body, a non-string bound route/query/header parameter or a required string query or header parameter. A route that requires authentication but performs no authority check declares 401 and not 403.** The OpenAPI document lists only declared responses, so an undeclared status is invisible to generated clients, and a 403 the handler can never return is false. *Check:* For new or changed routes, compare the statuses the handler returns or documents, and its bound parameters, against its declarations and its group's. Flag missing or duplicate 400s, a missing 412 or 415, and a 403 declared with no authority check. <sub>Identity ADR-1483; Identity ADR-1067; Identity outcomes of #599; Identity outcomes of #686; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **A problem response that asks the caller to wait sets the `Retry-After` header and a matching retry-after extension member. An operation refused because it came too soon after a previous one answers 409 with these. Losing a concurrency race answers 412.** Clients need a machine-readable signal for when to retry, and a lost race is a different failure from a rate limit. *Check:* Look for 429, 503 or 'too soon' problem responses without `Retry-After`, and for too-soon refusals mapped to the same status as concurrency conflicts. <sub>Identity ADR-1407; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Name a problem document's extension members through shared public constants, in writers and tests alike, not with string literals.** One set of names keeps writers, tests and client mirrors of the problem shape in agreement. *Check:* Look for string literals used as problem `Extensions` keys in production code or test assertions. <sub>Identity ADR-1483</sub>
- **A collection `GET` over a collection that can grow without bound returns one keyset page (`{ items, continuationToken }`), takes `cursor` and `limit` and clamps the limit to a default and a maximum. It never uses offset or skip paging and never returns the whole collection.** Offset paging skips or repeats rows under concurrent writes and slows as the offset grows. A keyset page has the same cost wherever it sits. *Check:* Look for list endpoints that return unbounded arrays, take `Skip`/`page`/`offset`, or don't clamp the limit. *Note:* Don't ask for paging on a collection that is small and bounded by design (such as an owner's secrets or a resource's scopes): returning it whole is intended. <sub>Identity ADR-1014</sub>
- **Expose list filters only as explicit, index-backed query parameters combined with AND, each backed by an explicit store method. Never add a general query protocol (OData, JSON:API filters, arbitrary sort or filter expressions, or `IQueryable` exposed or passed through).** Query protocols leak `IQueryable`, open a denial-of-service surface over the store, page by offset and become a heavyweight versioned contract. *Check:* Look for OData or JSON:API packages, filter or sort expression parameters, `IQueryable` crossing the API layer, and filters that no store index backs. <sub>Identity ADR-1014; Identity ADR-1020</sub>
- **An API that queries a date range must default the range when it is omitted and reject a range longer than a fixed maximum span.** Bounded ranges keep reads bounded however much history the store holds. *Check:* Look at endpoints taking from/to parameters for a missing default or a missing maximum-span check. <sub>Identity ADR-1199</sub>
- **Give an ETag or concurrency token only to a resource that is a stored, writable entity, and make the ETag depend only on that document. Expose caller-specific data (such as what the current caller may do) and merged or computed views from separate read-only resources without an ETag.** A merged view has nothing to write back, so a token guards nothing, and an ETag that varies with the caller can't serve as a document version. *Check:* Look for ETags or version fields on merged, effective or preview responses, and for permission or caller-derived properties added to an ETagged resource. <sub>Identity ADR-1204; Identity ADR-1418</sub>
- **Have the server compute whether the caller may make a change and expose it as one flag on the list response (such as `canChange`).
